messages.subject: trying to "colsplit" on a factor containing "."
messages.subject_clean: trying to "colsplit" on a factor containing "."
messages.body_plain:
This seems like it should be trivial but I haven't figured out a solution:

Works:
x <- c("a_1", "a_2", "b_2", "c_3")
varsx <- colsplit(x, "_", c("trt", "time"))
varsx
  trt time
1   a    1
2   a    2
3   b    2
4   c    3

Fails:
y <- c("a.1", "a.2", "b.2", "c.3")
varsy <- colsplit(x, ".", c("trt", "time"))
varsy
  trt time NA.
1  NA   NA  NA
2  NA   NA  NA
3  NA   NA  NA
4  NA   NA  NA

Any ideas?

Perhaps more importantly, can anyone point me at a good resource for doing basic string manipulations like this?  I seem run into issues of improper variable names, say containing "-" quite often and a primer on what the basic ground rules are for R would be helpful.

Thanks!

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I think the basic thing you're missing is that pattern (the second
argument to colsplit) is a regular expression. In regexp the . matches
any character, which is probably not what you want. To match a literal
. use \\. like this:

 varsy <- colsplit(y, "\\.", c("trt", "time"))

Best,
Ista

messages.body_plain:
Here we go, hopefully this is more useful

library(reshape)

# A function with 'validation'
    # The mean if length(x) > 100, otherwise NA
    mean2 <- function(x) if(length(x) >= 100)
                                        mean(x) else NA

# Generate some long format data to cast. Each level of the factor has 99
# values against it; mean2 on each should return NA both times.
test.df1 <- data.frame(  ctgry   = factor(rep(LETTERS[1:2], c(99,99))),
                         value   = rnorm(99 * 2)
                         )

# Fill argument not-supplied/NULL; A mixture of 0 and NA returned for two
# expected-to-be-NA results
cast(test.df1, ctgry ~., c(mean2, length), fill = NULL)
###      ctgry mean2 len2
###    1     A    NA   99
###    2     B     0   99

# Works as expected if fill = NA is given
cast(test.df1, ctgry ~., c(mean2, length), fill = NA)
###      ctgry mean2 len2
###    1     A    NA   99
###    2     B    NA   99

# Supplying a single aggregation function doesn't appear problematic in
# this instance
cast(test.df1, ctgry ~., mean2, fill = NULL)
###      ctgry (all)
###    1     A    NA
###    2     B    NA

# An unlikely analysis problem!
func <- function(x) {if(1 > 2) 0 else NA}

cast(test.df1, ctgry ~., c(func, length))
###      ctgry func length
###    1     A   NA     99
###    2     B    0     99

messages.subject_clean: bug in aaply? Why does aaply(data,2,class) returns “data.frame” for all columns?
messages.body_plain:
Hi, I was playing around with the plyr function and discovered that aaply(data,2,class) returns a vector of length ncol(data) filled with “data.frame”. I would expect that it returns a vector with the class of the variables in the dataframe. As a consequence, testing which columns are numerical also fails. Below is some code to illustrate my point.

Thanks and best!

ps: I started the discussion here http://stackoverflow.com/q/10673771/1318686 and someone pointed me to this list noting "It [the help page] says that dataframe input should be accepted [for a*ply functions] and that an array should be the output. So you have discovered either an error in the documentation or a bug in the function"

data=data.frame(str=rep("str",3),num=c(1:3))

class(data[,1])
# "factor
class(data[,2])
# "integer"

aaply(data,2,class)
# "data.frame" "data.frame"
aaply(data,2,is.numeric)
# FALSE FALSE

messages.subject: R development master class: NYC June 21-22, Bay Area June 28-29
messages.subject_clean: R development master class: NYC June 21-22, Bay Area June 28-29
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm going to be teaching an R development master classes in NYC June
21-12 and in the Bay Area June 28-29. The basic idea of the class is
to help you write better code, focused on the mantra of "do not repeat
yourself". In day one you will learn powerful new tools of
abstraction, allowing you to solve a wider range of problems with
fewer lines of code. Day two will teach you how to make packages, the
fundamental unit of code distribution in R, allowing others to save
time by allowing them to use your code.

To get the most out of this course, you should have some experience
programming in R already: you should be familiar with writing
functions, and the basic data structures of R: vectors, matrices,
arrays, lists and data frames. You will find the course particularly
useful if you're an experienced R user looking to take the next step,
or if you're moving to R from other programming languages and you want
to quickly get up to speed with R's unique features. You can see the
material we covered last time at http://bit.ly/odi3ai.

Both days will incorporate a mix of lectures and hands-on learning. Expect to
learn about a topic and then immediately put it into practice with a small
example. Plenty of help will be available if you get stuck. You'll receive a
printed copy of all slides, as well as electronic access to the slides, code
and data. The material covered in the course is currently being turned into a
book: you can access the current draft at http://bit.ly/dDv5rt.

To see prices, locations and register, please see:
http://bit.ly/lTft9e. Early bird discounts available until May 31, and
limited discounts for students (66% off) and academics (33% off) are
available - please contact me for details.

Regards,

Hadley

--
Assistant Professor / Dobelman Family Junior Chair
Department of Statistics / Rice University
http://had.co.nz/

messages.subject: ddply() seems to be stuck
messages.body_plain:
I have a situation where I asked ddply() to crunch I rather large data set.  ("How large?" you ask?  I can't tell you at the moment because it's stuck!  Probably ~1M records)  I turned on the text progress bar and it got to 25% but has been hanging out there for 2 days.  Although it was doing some work in parallel initially it seems to be in a serial phase because only one core is active.  Lack of memory is not the issue either.  Has anyone else ever experienced this?  Could it be that the children that were spawned for the parallel work died ungracefully and the parent is waiting for returns that are never going to happen?  I would be glad to provide more details but this may be one that is difficult to reproduce unless you want to step through my massive processing workflow.  If anyone has any thoughts I am all ears.  Thanks.

Neil Best

Computation Institute
University of Chicago
